units.title: How Words Are Built
units.blurb: Prefixes, roots and suffixes, and where they come from.

units.title: Not, Good and Bad
units.blurb: The prefixes that say no, and the ones that say good or bad.

units.title: Where and When
units.blurb: Prefixes of place and time: before and after, under and over, between, across, out and back.

units.title: Together, Against and How Many
units.blurb: Prefixes for with and against, toward and away, one and all, and how prefixes change shape.

units.title: Latin Roots
units.blurb: The Latin roots that build the most English words: say, see, believe, go, throw, lead, turn, hold, run and more.

units.blurb: Greek roots for time, feeling, words, rule and form.

units.title: Suffixes
units.blurb: Endings that turn a root into an adjective, a noun or a verb.

topics.title: Prefix, Root and Suffix
topics.short: Most long words are built from parts: a prefix in front, a root in the middle and a suffix at the end.
topics.trouble: Learners split words by spelling alone (seeing "pen" in "repent") or assume every word with a familiar part carries its meaning. A root is a clue to check against the sentence, not a guarantee.

topics.title: Latin and Greek: Where the Parts Come From
topics.short: Many English words come from Latin, often by way of French, and many learned and scientific words come from Greek.
topics.trouble: Learners treat all roots as Latin. ph, ch (said like k), y and th inside a root are clues to Greek (philanthropist, chronic, synchronize, pathos); some words even mix the two languages.

topics.title: Not: in-, un- and non-
topics.short: in-, un- and non- turn a word into its opposite; in- changes to im-, il- and ir- to fit the next sound.
topics.trouble: Not every in- means not: in- also means in or into (inhale, incite), and inflammable means easily set on fire.

topics.title: Without: a- and an-
topics.short: In words from Greek, a- (an- before a vowel) means without or not.
topics.trouble: a- means without only in Greek-based words (apathy, anarchy); in English words like asleep and aboard, a- means on or in.

topics.title: Good and Bad: bene- and mal-
topics.short: bene- means well and mal- means badly.
topics.trouble: Not every word that starts with ben- or mal- has these parts: bench and mall do not.

topics.title: Good and Bad in Greek: eu- and dys-
topics.short: eu- means good or well and dys- means bad or difficult, in words from Greek.
topics.trouble: Learners confuse eulogy (praise) with elegy (a sad poem). eu- is a clue only at the start of a word.

topics.title: Wrongly and Apart: mis- and dis-
topics.short: mis- means wrongly; dis- means apart, away or not.
topics.trouble: Greek mis- or miso- means hate (misanthrope) and is a different part from the English mis- that means wrongly (mistake). dis- can mean not (dishonest), apart (dissect) or away (dismiss).

topics.title: Before and After: pre-, ante- and post-
topics.short: pre- and ante- mean before; post- means after.
topics.trouble: ante- (before) is not anti- (against): antecedent comes before, antidote works against. posthumous looks like post- + humus, but it comes from Latin postumus, "last."

topics.title: Under and Over: sub-, super-, hypo- and hyper-
topics.short: sub- and hypo- mean under; super- and hyper- mean over or beyond.
topics.trouble: sub- changes shape before some letters: suc-, sup-, sur-, sus- (succumb, suppress, surreptitious, sustain). sur- can also come from super- (surplus, surfeit).

topics.title: Between, Within and Around: inter-, intro-, circum- and peri-
topics.short: inter- means between, intro- and intra- mean within, and circum- and peri- mean around.
topics.trouble: inter- (between) is not intra- (within): an interstate highway crosses states; intrastate travel stays inside one.

topics.title: Across and Through: trans-, per- and dia-
topics.short: trans- means across or beyond; per- and dia- mean through.
topics.trouble: per- often just strengthens a word, meaning thoroughly rather than through (perturb, persistent).

topics.title: Out and In: ex-, e-, in- and en-
topics.short: ex- and e- mean out; in-, im-, en- and em- mean in or into.
topics.trouble: ex- shrinks to e- before many consonants (elicit, evasive, eminent) and becomes ef- before f (effrontery). The in- that means into is a different prefix from the in- that means not.

topics.title: Back, Again and Down: re- and de-
topics.short: re- means back or again; de- means down, away or completely.
topics.trouble: re- does not always mean again: in reticent, reclusive and relinquish it means back or away. de- can mean down, away from or completely.

topics.title: Together: con-, com- and syn-
topics.short: con- (Latin) and syn- (Greek) mean with or together.
topics.trouble: con- changes to com-, col-, cor- and co- to fit the next sound; syn- changes to sym- and syl-. Sometimes con- only strengthens a word, meaning thoroughly (confound).

topics.title: Against: contra-, anti- and ob-
topics.short: contra-, counter-, anti- and ob- all carry the idea of against.
topics.trouble: anti- (against) is not ante- (before). ob- hides in shapes like oc-, of- and op- (occur, offer, oppose).

topics.title: Away, Toward and Forward: ab-, ad- and pro-
topics.short: ab- means away, ad- means toward and pro- means forward.
topics.trouble: ad- changes to fit the next letter: ac-, af-, ag-, al-, an-, ap-, ar-, as-, at- (accede, affable, aggregate, alleviate). A doubled letter after a- is the clue.

topics.title: How Many: mono-, uni-, di- and poly-
topics.short: Number prefixes come in Greek and Latin pairs: mono- and uni- (one), di- and bi- (two), poly- and multi- (many).
topics.trouble: Learners mix the Greek and Latin sets; both are right in their own words (monorail, unicycle).

topics.title: All and Both: omni-, pan- and ambi-
topics.short: omni- (Latin) and pan- (Greek) mean all; ambi- means both.
topics.trouble: pan- means all only in Greek-based words (panorama, panacea); it has nothing to do with a cooking pan.

topics.title: Prefixes That Change Shape
topics.short: Many prefixes change their last letter to match the root that follows: in- to im-, con- to col-, ad- to ac-, sub- to sup-.
topics.trouble: A doubled consonant after a short prefix (acc-, aff-, coll-, imm-, irr-, supp-) is often the sign of a prefix that changed its last letter.

topics.title: Say, Speak and Call: dict, loqu, voc, nounce and mand
topics.short: dict means say, loqu means speak, voc means call, nounce means announce and mand means order.
topics.trouble: dict hides in verdict (ver + dict: a true saying) and indict, said in-DITE.

topics.title: Look and See: spec, spic, vid and vis
topics.short: spec and spic mean look; vid and vis mean see.
topics.trouble: The root also hides inside words that no longer feel like "seeing" words, like auspicious (from watching birds) and specious (from appearance).

topics.title: Believe, Trust, True and Know: cred, fid, ver and sci
topics.short: cred means believe, fid means trust, ver means true and sci means know.
topics.trouble: fid shrinks in diffident (dis + fid), and ver hides in verdict. credulous (too ready to believe) and incredulous (not believing) are near opposites.

topics.title: Go and Step: ced, cess, gress and grad
topics.short: ced, ceed and cess mean go or yield; gress and grad mean step.
topics.trouble: Three spellings, one root: -cede (concede), -ceed (proceed, succeed, exceed) and -cess (excess). supersede is the odd one out: it comes from a different root, sed (sit).

topics.title: Throw and Send: ject, mit and miss
topics.short: ject means throw; mit and miss mean send or let go.
topics.trouble: Learners miss the root when the prefix changes it: submit (sub + mit), demise (de + mit).

topics.title: Lead, Pull and Shut: duc, tract and clud
topics.short: duc means lead, tract means pull and clud and clus mean shut.
topics.trouble: tract (pull) also names a stretch of land or a pamphlet; the root idea is "drawn out."

topics.title: Turn: vert and vers
topics.short: vert and vers mean turn.
topics.trouble: adverse (harmful) and averse (unwilling) share the root but are different words; both come from turning against or away.

topics.title: Peace, Pleasing and War: pac, plac and bell
topics.short: pac means peace, plac means please or calm and bell means war.
topics.trouble: bell (war) is not the bell you ring or belle (a beauty): belligerent means warlike.

topics.title: Flocks, Friends and Hearts: greg, am, cord and sent
topics.short: greg means flock, am means love or friend, cord means heart and sent means feel.
topics.trouble: inimical hides am (in + amicus, "not friendly"). egregious once meant standing out from the flock in a good way.

topics.title: Hold, Hang, Carry and Pour: ten, pend, fer and fund
topics.short: ten means hold, pend means hang or weigh, fer means carry and fund and fus mean pour.
topics.trouble: tain and tin are the same root as ten (contain, abstain); pensive comes from weighing thoughts.

topics.title: Run, Follow, Walk and Flee: cur, sequ, ped and fug
topics.short: cur means run, sequ means follow, ped means foot and fug means flee.
topics.trouble: ped (foot, Latin) is not ped (child, Greek, as in pediatrics). cursory has nothing to do with cursing: a cursory look runs over things.

topics.title: Light and Heavy: luc, lev and grav
topics.short: luc means light (brightness), lev means light (not heavy) and grav means heavy.
topics.trouble: Two different "lights": luc is about brightness (lucid), lev about weight (levity, alleviate).

topics.title: Life, Food and Sleep: viv, vor and somn
topics.short: viv and vit mean life, vor means eat and somn means sleep.
topics.trouble: soporific comes from a related word, sopor (deep sleep). voracious is used for appetites of every kind, not only for food.

topics.title: Time: chron, temp, ann and nov
topics.short: chron (Greek) and temp (Latin) mean time, ann and enn mean year, and nov means new.
topics.trouble: chronic means long-lasting, not severe; perennial hides enn (per + annus, "through the years").

topics.title: Feeling, Love and Humankind: path, phil, miso and anthrop
topics.short: path means feeling, phil means love, miso means hate and anthrop means human being.
topics.trouble: empathy (feeling with someone) is not sympathy (feeling sorry for someone), and apathy (no feeling) is not antipathy (dislike).

topics.title: Word and Writing: log and graph
topics.short: log means word, reason or study; graph and gram mean write or draw.
topics.trouble: -logy means "the study of" in most science words (biology), but log alone often means word or speech (eulogy, dialogue).

topics.title: Rule: -cracy, -archy and auto-
topics.short: -cracy and -crat mean rule or power, -archy and -arch mean rule or chief, and auto- means self.
topics.trouble: arch can also mean first or chief (archetype, archenemy), not only rule.

topics.title: Birth, Kind and Form: gen and morph
topics.short: gen means birth, kind or produce; morph means form or shape.
topics.trouble: gen appears in very different-looking words: genesis, ingenious, ingenuous, engender and genial all trace back to it.

topics.title: Adjective Endings: -ous, -ive, -ible and -ic
topics.short: Endings like -ous (full of), -ive (tending to), -ible and -able (able to be) and -ic (having to do with) make adjectives.
topics.trouble: The ending tells the part of speech, not the meaning: copious, pernicious and impetuous are all adjectives but mean very different things.

topics.title: Noun Endings: -ity, -tion, -ance, -ism and -ist
topics.short: Endings like -ity, -tion, -ance and -ence name a quality or an act; -ism names a belief and -ist a person.
topics.trouble: A noun ending changes how a word fits a sentence: veracity (a noun) is not veracious (an adjective).

topics.title: Verb Endings: -ate, -ify and -ize
topics.short: Endings like -ate, -ify and -ize make verbs that mean to make or to act.
topics.trouble: Not every word ending in -ate is a verb: considerate and obstinate are adjectives, and the -ate is said differently (-it, not -ate).
